questions.explanation: Negative indexing: -1 is last (50), -2 is second from last (40).
Slicing [1:4] returns elements at index 1, 2, 3 (stop is exclusive). So [2, 3, 4].

questions.text: What is the key difference between a list and a tuple?
options: Tuples are faster; lists allow duplicates
Lists are mutable; tuples are immutable
Lists are ordered; tuples are unordered
questions.explanation: The core difference: lists are mutable (can be changed), tuples are immutable (cannot be changed after creation). Both are ordered and allow duplicates.
dict.get(key, default) returns the default if the key is not found, instead of raising a KeyError. 'd' is not in the dict, so 99 is returned.
sort() modifies the list in place. After sorting: [1,1,3,4,5,9]. First element is 1, last is 9.
& is set intersection — elements in both sets. {1,2,3} & {2,3,4} = {2,3}.
Tuples are immutable. Attempting to change an element raises TypeError: 'tuple' object does not support item assignment.

questions.text: What does this list comprehension produce?
questions.code: result = [x**2 for x in range(5) if x % 2 != 0]
questions.explanation: range(5) = 0,1,2,3,4. Filter odd numbers (x%2!=0): 1,3. Then square them: 1,9.
[::2] means start to end with step 2. Picks every other element: 'a'(0), 'c'(2), 'e'(4).

questions.text: Which method removes and returns the last element of a list?
questions.explanation: pop() removes and returns the last element (or element at a given index). remove() removes by value. discard() is a set method.
Dictionaries use unique keys. Assigning to 'x' twice overwrites the first value. Final dict has 2 keys: x=30, y=20.
Sets automatically remove duplicates. {1,2,2,3,3,3} becomes {1,2,3}, which has 3 elements.
[::-1] is the idiom for reversing a list. Step of -1 traverses from end to start.

questions.text: Which statement about dict.items() is correct?
options: Returns a list of keys only
Returns a list of values only
Returns a view of (key, value) tuples
Returns a sorted list of keys
questions.explanation: dict.items() returns a view object of (key, value) pairs that can be iterated. Use list(d.items()) to get a concrete list.
b = a makes b point to the same list object (not a copy). Modifying b also modifies a. Use b = a.copy() or b = a[:] for an independent copy.
